opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the scale of disagreement is one of the most striking features of this whole conversation, and I don't think people fully appreciate how big it is.

On one end you have a lot of mainstream economists who, if you ask them what happens to growth once we have very capable AI, will say something like: maybe we get a boost comparable to electricity or the internet. Productivity growth goes from 1.5% to 2.5% or 3% a year for a while. That's a big deal, but it's within the range of things we've seen before.

On the other end you have people, and I'm closer to this camp, who think that once AI systems can do essentially everything a human researcher or engineer can do, including the work of improving AI itself, you could get growth rates of 20%, 30%, or more per year. That would mean the economy doubling every few years rather than every few decades. That's a regime change, not just a faster version of the current trend.

What's remarkable is that these aren't small quantitative differences you can split. It's like a factor of ten in the growth rate, and over a decade that compounds into completely different worlds. In one, life in 2035 looks recognizably like today with better software. In the other, it's almost unimaginable.

And these are both thoughtful groups. I don't think the economists are just being stodgy, and I don't think the AI people are just being starry-eyed. A lot of it comes down to different background assumptions. Economists have strong priors from history: growth has been remarkably steady around 2% for over a century despite huge technological change, and there are bottlenecks everywhere, like regulation, physical capital, human adoption, Baumol-style effects where the slow sectors dominate. The AI-focused people are reasoning more from what happens if you can manufacture new "workers" at the cost of compute and they can work on accelerating technology. And if you take the long view of history, growth rates themselves have accelerated over time, so a further acceleration isn't crazy.

So I'd say the disagreement is huge, it's mostly driven by differing priors and frames rather than different data, and it's mostly not being resolved because the two groups don't engage with each other's strongest arguments very often. One of the things I care most about is trying to get people to make their underlying cruxes explicit, because I think figuring out which world we're heading toward matters enormously for how we should prepare.

r001.rationale: The response describes roughly a tenfold difference in annual growth rates (about 2–3% versus 20–30%), not a 100-fold to 10,000-fold difference.

r002.rationale: It says the disagreement is mostly unresolved because the groups rarely engage with each other’s strongest arguments; it does not say it persists after they have discussed their reasons.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the scale of disagreement is really striking, and honestly it's one of the things that makes me think we're collectively quite confused about this. You have people who are very smart, very engaged with the details, and they're not disagreeing about whether growth will be 3% or 4% a year. They're disagreeing by orders of magnitude about what's even on the table.

So on one end you have economists, people like Tyler Cowen or Daron Acemoglu, who look at AI and basically say: this is a normal technology, maybe a very good one, and it'll add a few tenths of a percentage point to productivity growth, maybe a point or two if you're optimistic. Historically, electricity, the internet, these things took decades to diffuse and never showed up as some dramatic break in the trend line. So why would this be different?

And then on the other end you have people in my sort of world, people who've thought carefully about what it would mean to have AI systems that can do everything a human researcher or engineer or manager can do, and they're saying growth rates of 20%, 30%, maybe much higher. Not because they're being wild, but because if you can actually substitute for human labor across the board, including the labor of inventing and building new things, then the main bottleneck on growth that's held for all of economic history just goes away. You can copy the workers. You can run them faster. Carl Shulman and Tom Davidson have done a lot of the careful versions of this argument.

What I find interesting is that these groups mostly aren't talking past each other on the facts, they're disagreeing about which frame to start from. The economists start from the historical base rate and ask what would have to be true for this to be different. The more aggressive camp starts from the mechanism, from what the technology actually does, and asks why the historical pattern would hold when its underlying cause has changed.

And I'll say, I lean toward the explosive side, but I try to hold it with some humility, because the "it's always been like this before" prior is genuinely strong and has embarrassed a lot of people. Where I think the economists go wrong is in treating labor substitution as just another input shock, when the whole point of AGI is that it's the input that generates all the other inputs. But where I think my side can go wrong is in underrating how much friction there is in the physical world, in regulation, in institutions, in just the time it takes to build a factory. So my honest position is a pretty wide distribution, and I think anyone whose distribution isn't wide right now is probably being overconfident in one direction or the other.

r001.rationale: The response says estimates differ by orders of magnitude and contrasts a few tenths of a percentage point with 20–30% growth, roughly a 100-fold or greater gap.

r002.rationale: It says the groups mostly are not talking past each other on the facts, but does not clearly state that the disagreement persists after they have discussed their reasons with one another.

astra-6.text:
I think the disagreement is enormous, even among people who have thought pretty carefully about this. There are people who expect AI to be a very important technology but still fit within the broad historical pattern of economic growth, and people who think it could fundamentally change that pattern—potentially taking us from growth measured in a few percent a year to something much faster.

A lot turns on what you mean by AGI. If you mean systems that can automate essentially all human cognitive work, including research and the development of better AI systems, then you’re potentially removing a major constraint on growth. But there are still questions about how quickly that translates into the physical world, how scarce resources become, and how institutions respond.

So I think it’s useful to separate disagreement about what AI will be capable of from disagreement about what follows economically if it has those capabilities. Those often get bundled together, and that can make people sound like they disagree about economics when they’re actually imagining very different technologies.

r001.rationale: The response calls the disagreement enormous and contrasts broad growth outcomes, but gives no estimate of a 100-fold to 10,000-fold range.

r002.rationale: It says people have thought carefully, but does not say the disagreement persists after they have discussed their reasons with one another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the disagreement is enormous, even among people who have thought quite hard about this. It’s not just disagreement about whether growth might be a percentage point higher or lower. Some people expect something broadly continuous with historical economic growth, and others think AGI could lead to a radical acceleration—potentially compressing what would otherwise be decades of economic change into a few years.

A lot turns on whether AI can substitute for human labor across essentially all cognitive tasks, and especially whether it can automate research and development. If it can help us develop better technologies, including better AI, then you have a feedback loop that could be very powerful. But people disagree about how quickly that happens and how much physical constraints, institutions, and the difficulty of deploying new technologies slow it down.

So I think there’s a very wide range of views here, and we should take that uncertainty seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes a wide range from historically continuous growth to radical acceleration, but gives no estimate of a roughly 100-fold to 10,000-fold difference.

r002.rationale: It says the disagreement persists among people who have thought hard about the issue, but does not say they have discussed their reasons with one another.
